title: Who deserves respect
hookLine: teachers free of greed, hate and delusion deserve respect

lines: A QUESTION TO BE READY FOR.
cards: How do you decide whose advice to trust? Follower counts? A title?

A confident voice? In the hundred and fiftieth discourse, the Buddha is walking through Kosala with a large company of monks and stops at a brahmin village called Nagaravinda. The householders come out to meet him.
Some bow. Some just exchange polite greetings. Some sit down in silence.
And he gives them a question to be ready for, because wanderers from other groups may well ask it.

teach.b: Suppose, the Buddha says, wanderers of other groups ask you: which recluses and brahmins should not be honored or respected? Answer like this.

Those who aren't free of greed, hate and delusion for what the eye sees, the ear hears, and the rest. Whose minds aren't at peace inside. Who act well one day and badly the next, in body, speech and mind.
Why not honor them? Because, the householders would say, we're like that ourselves; we see nothing higher in them. And which should be honored?

Those free of greed, hate and delusion toward what the senses bring, whose minds are at peace, who act well steadily, in body, speech and mind. Because we see something higher in them than in ourselves.
Notice what's missing. No mention of robes.
No mention of which teacher someone follows, or which group. The test makes no exception for the Buddha's own monks.
The measure is the same for everyone: what has this person done with greed, hate and delusion? The Pali words are lobha, dosa, moha, the three roots the discourses keep returning to.
Then the Buddha supplies the next question those wanderers would ask. How would you know? What's the evidence?
Look at how they live. Such teachers go to the forest, to remote places, where there are no sights or sounds or tastes to delight in. They choose the quiet, and you can see the choice.
So respect isn't about rank, and it isn't blind. It's earned by a visible life, and you're allowed to watch before you give it.

how: In Buddhist communities respect for teachers is shown through bowing, offerings and service; the discourses also encourage lay people to watch a teacher's conduct over time, as in MN 150 and MN 47, before placing trust.

o: greed, one of the three unwholesome roots
a monk's begging bowl for food
anger that flares up at an insult

games.q: who deserves respect: tap the pairs.

s: MN 150 tells the villagers to honor only the Buddha's monks
the test is the same for everyone: freedom from greed, hate and delusion, seen in conduct.
the villagers are told to give a reason for their respect
they would say: we see something higher in them than in ourselves.
the evidence offered is the teachers' choice of quiet, remote places
they live where there's nothing for the senses to delight in.

games.q: you're a householder in Nagaravinda. wandering teachers ask: which recluses deserve your respect? what does the Buddha tell you to answer?
o: those free of greed, hate and delusion, whose minds are at peace.
those who belong to the Buddha's order.
games.why: he gives a test anyone can apply to anyone, including his own monks: what have they done with greed, hate and delusion, and does their life show it?

practice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something without trying to be admired: a grandparent, a coach, a nurse, a friend.
Picture how they lived, what they didn't grab, what they didn't hate, what they saw clearly, and let a little gratitude rise. If you like, bow your head slightly, inside or out.

wordCard.voice: Lobha. Greed, one of the three roots along with dosa and moha: not the title or the group, but the one free of all three, and you can see it in how they live. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali lobha, dosa, moha: greed, hate, delusion, the three roots. the measure of a teacher in MN 150.

carryVoice: Your line: who to respect. Confidence is easy to see; a steady, quiet life takes longer. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 150, Nagaravindeyya Sutta (to the people of Nagaravinda)
